prime.problem: The output layer logits = h @ W2 + b2 mixes whole matrices, so the scalar chain rule from micrograd doesn't say directly which matrix to multiply by which, or where the transpose goes. Get the order wrong and the code either crashes or, worse, runs and gives wrong gradients.
prime.fits: You've just backpropagated through the softmax chain down to dlogits, and seen that a broadcast forward becomes a sum backward. This card crosses the first linear layer and hands dh on to tanh and BatchNorm. Linear layer 1 on the embedding card reuses exactly the same three lines.
expect: the transpose and the inner dimension of a matmul
the bias gradient as a sum over the batch
shape matching as a derivation shortcut
prime.goal: Derive the matmul backward on a 2×2 example, then write dh, dW2 and db2 from the shapes alone and know when shapes are not enough.

attend: In the 2×2 example, why does dL/da11 use a row of B rather than a column, and how does that turn into B.T?
Which dimension gets summed away in h.T @ dlogits, and what does that sum mean in terms of the 32 examples?
Why is db2 a sum over dim 0 and not a copy of one row of dlogits?
Why does shape matching give exactly one answer for this layer, and what property of 32, 64 and 27 makes that true?
How many multiply-adds does each backward matmul cost compared with the forward matmul?

must: aij multiplies row j of B in every entry of row i of D → the chain rule sums dDik·Bjk over k → that is row i of dD dotted with row j of B → dA = dD @ B.T (and by symmetry dB = A.T @ dD)
Every dX has the shape of X → only one way to combine dlogits (32,27) with W2 (64,27) into (32,64) → the 27s must meet, so W2 is transposed → dh = dlogits @ W2.T falls out without calculus
W2 and b2 are reused by all 32 rows of the batch → a forward reuse becomes a backward sum → dW2 contracts over the 32 examples (h.T @ dlogits) and db2 = dlogits.sum(0)

Shape matching only picks the arrangement when the dimensions differ → equal dimensions (a square weight, or the 2×2 example) let a wrong formula have the right shape → it runs silently, so derive or cmp
elevated: Each backward matmul does the same work as the forward one (32·64·27 = 55,296 multiply-adds) → a linear layer's backward pass costs about twice its forward pass, and no Jacobian (1,769,472 numbers for dlogits/dh) is ever built
reference: the exact PyTorch error text for mismatched shapes (mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied)
the lab's trick L = (D * dD).sum() to inject an arbitrary upstream gradient
the toy matrices A, B, c, dD used in the 2×2 example

compress.prompt: From memory, draw logits = h @ W2 + b2 with every shape, then write the three backward lines and, next to each, which dimension is summed away and why. Or explain in 3–5 sentences where the transpose in dh = dlogits @ W2.T comes from.
checklist: each gradient has the shape of its tensor: dh (32,64), dW2 (64,27), db2 (27,)
dh = dlogits @ W2.T: sums over the 27 logits
dW2 = h.T @ dlogits: sums over the 32 examples, because W2 is shared by every row
db2 = dlogits.sum(0): b2 was broadcast down the batch
the transpose appears because each input entry is dotted with a row of the other matrix (the 2×2 derivation)
shape matching works only when the dimensions are all different

retrieve.q: Explain, without quoting the formula, why the gradient of the left matrix in a matmul ends up multiplied by the transpose of the right one.
answer: a<sub>ij</sub> contributes to every entry D<sub>ik</sub> in row i, each time multiplied by B<sub>jk</sub>
the chain rule adds those uses: Σ<sub>k</sub> dD<sub>ik</sub>·B<sub>jk</sub>
that pairs row i of dD with row j of B, which is what dD @ B.T computes

retrieve.q: Walk through deriving dW2 from shapes alone: what must its shape be, which two tensors can you use, and how do you arrange them?
answer: dW2 must be (64,27), the shape of W2
available: h (32,64) and dlogits (32,27)
the shared 32 must be the inner dimension, so transpose h: (64,32) @ (32,27) = h.T @ dlogits
summing over the 32 is adding up every example's contribution to the shared weight

retrieve.q: With the 2×2 example A=[[1,2],[3,4]], B=[[5,6],[7,8]], dD=[[1,0],[2,−1]], compute dA[2,1] and dc by hand.
You're backpropagating through a layer whose weight is 64×64 with a batch of 64. Can you still rely on shape matching? What would you do instead, and what does it cost?
answer: no: dD @ W and dD @ W.T both have the right shape, and so do several other arrangements
derive it (the 2×2 argument generalises) or check each candidate with cmp against autograd
the cost is a derivation or one extra autograd run, which is cheap next to a silently wrong gradient

compare.q: db2 = dlogits.sum(0) and dW2 = h.T @ dlogits both add up over the batch. How is the bias case an instance of the sum/broadcast duality, and how does the matmul hide the same sum inside its inner dimension?
answer: b2 is broadcast (copied) to 32 rows forward, so its gradient sums the 32 rows backward
W2 is also reused by all 32 rows; the matmul h.T @ dlogits performs that sum as its inner-dimension contraction
both come from the same rule: a value used many times collects the sum of its gradients
failure mode for both: forget the sum (or the transpose) and you get a shape error or a per-example gradient

compare.q: The toolkit card used shapes to check a forward matmul; this card uses them to choose a backward formula. What extra rule makes the backward use possible, and where does it stop working?
answer: the extra rule: every gradient has the same shape as the tensor it belongs to
forward: shapes confirm an expression is valid; backward: they also pin down the only valid arrangement
stops working when dimensions coincide, because then several arrangements fit

compare.q: Crossing the linear layer takes three lines found from shapes; crossing tanh needs (1 - h**2) * dh. Why can't shapes derive the tanh line, and what kind of knowledge does it need instead?
answer: tanh is elementwise: input, output and gradient all have the same shape, so shapes don't constrain anything
you need the local derivative of tanh (1 − tanh²), which is calculus, not bookkeeping
matmul backward is determined by structure; elementwise backward is determined by the function

predict.q: Suppose n_hidden were 27 instead of 64, so W2 is a square 27×27 matrix. You mistakenly write dh = dlogits @ W2 (no transpose). What happens when it runs, and what catches the mistake?
predict.answer: It runs without any error: (32,27) @ (27,27) gives (32,27), which is exactly h.shape. The values are wrong unless W2 happens to be symmetric. Shape matching can't see it, so only the derivation or cmp (exact: False, approximate: False) catches it. That's why Karpathy keeps the dimensions distinct and checks every line.
